before_faq: It shows Saturn, the Roman god often folded together with Greece's Titan Cronus, biting into the body of his own son. Goya applied it straight onto a wall inside his own home sometime between 1819 and 1823, part of a set of fourteen wall murals that collectively go by the name Black Paintings. Restorers moved it onto canvas later, and it hangs today at Madrid's Museo del Prado, catalogued as P00763, at roughly 143.5×81.4 cm.

No. They are two different works; Madrid's Prado museum owns both. Peter Paul Rubens painted his version in the late 1630s, commissioned to decorate a hunting retreat, showing Saturn as a controlled figure, posed the way classical sculpture would pose him, biting into a clearly living infant. Goya's version, painted nearly two centuries later for his own house rather than a patron, strips away the setting and focuses almost entirely on Saturn's wild-eyed face and a child whose body has already lost any recognizable features.

Yes, originally. Goya put brush directly onto plaster within Quinta del Sordo, his own Madrid home, sometime in the years spanning roughly 1819 to 1823. After his death, the house's new owner, financier d'Erlanger, hired a restorer to peel every one of the wall murals free and move them onto canvas over four years in the mid-1870s so they could be exhibited in Paris. Wreckers leveled the house itself in 1909; the canvas now in the Prado is the only form the image survives in.

Almost certainly, according to the great majority of Goya scholars and the Prado's own catalogue record, though the attribution has been formally challenged. In 2003, Junquera, a Madrid-based art historian, pointed to property deeds suggesting part of the house went up after Goya left Spain in 1824, and proposed that Goya's son or grandson may have been the one holding the brush instead. Most specialists, Nigel Glendinning among them, pushed back, arguing the documents don't prove much either way, and no lab test has ever settled it for certain.

There is no single confirmed meaning. Proposed readings include a political allegory for a country consuming its own people during Spain's civil conflicts of the early 1820s, a personal meditation on mortality and ageing, since Goya began the series at 73 shortly after a near-fatal illness, and a more general commentary on destructive paternal authority. Goya left no writing explaining the series, so all three readings remain interpretive rather than documented.
At the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid, on view continuously since 1889, alongside its thirteen companion murals and Rubens's earlier take on the same subject.

Fourteen made it into the Prado's holdings, but Antonio Brugada, who painted and knew Goya personally, catalogued fifteen murals across the house's two floors in 1828. Charles Yriarte, a French critic who toured the house in 1867, described one more mural that was gone from the wall by then. Most point to a mural of five faces set against a mountain backdrop, held today by a private collector in New York; its paper trail can be traced as far back as an 1846 Madrid palace inventory, though some scholars have questioned whether it is authentically Goya's work.

An unidentified illness struck him in late 1792 and nearly killed him, leaving him permanently deaf; researchers have proposed causes ranging from lead poisoning in his paints to a viral or autoimmune condition, but no diagnosis has ever been confirmed. The same illness recurred in 1819, again nearly fatally, not long before Goya started this mural series on his own plaster.

People who get this image tattooed are usually drawing on the same readings art historians have proposed for the painting itself: time as a devouring force that consumes everything, including youth, or a symbol of destructive power that will do anything, even destroy what it created, to hold on to control. Some tattoo write-ups also connect it to personal fears about aging and mortality, the same anxieties historians think Goya may have been working through when he painted it in his seventies after a near-fatal illness. None of these readings is Goya's own recorded explanation, since he never wrote a word about this mural series; they're later interpretations, same as the ones applied to the original canvas.

before_faq: No. Speaking to an interviewer in 1969, in a remark the Warhol Museum quotes, Warhol said he preferred working through a screen precisely because it meant he did not have to touch his own pictures at all, adding that any assistant could recreate his artwork just as well as he could. His chief studio assistant through most of that decade, Gerard Malanga, prepared and inked screens and pulled the prints that finished the canvas using a screen supplied by an outside vendor.

Collector Joe Simon-Whelan sued the Warhol Foundation along with the panel that authenticated his work and related parties, for $20 million in late 2007, after that panel rejected his 1965 canvas twice, in 2002 and 2003. He abandoned the suit in 2010 once he could no longer afford to keep funding the litigation, and the case never reached a court ruling on the painting's authenticity. A different canvas from the same 1965 batch, owned by Richard Ekstract, was later consigned to a 2022 auction backed by an outside expert's opinion that it was genuine.

No. By early 2012 the Foundation shut its official authenticating panel down entirely, a body that had ruled on Warhol's work for sixteen years, after the Simon-Whelan lawsuit cost it upward of $7 million to fight. It still runs a separate scholarly catalogue project of Warhol's work, but says that effort is not meant to serve the art market. Authentication now happens through independent specialists, such as Richard Polsky, working privately rather than through any panel tied to the Foundation.

Joel Wachs, the Foundation's president, said the board's legal costs, over $7 million spent fighting a single lawsuit brought by collector Joe Simon-Whelan, had become a drain on money that should go to artists. The Art Newspaper's report of the closure ran 28 October 2011, with the board set to shut by early 2012. The Foundation's decision also led the separate boards that vetted Basquiat's and Haring's work to shut down in the year after, for fear of facing similar suits.

His first solo pop-art show opened 9 July 1962 in Los Angeles, at Ferus, the gallery Irving Blum ran, presenting one canvas for every flavour then sold in Campbell's product line, 32 in total, displayed on narrow ledges in a single row. Asked why 32, Warhol reportedly gave gallery director Irving Blum a one-line answer citing the number of soup flavours itself. Some early reviewers compared it to a supermarket shelf rather than serious painting.

Cardiac arrhythmia, in the early hours of 22 February 1987, two days after gallbladder surgery at New York Hospital that his doctors had called routine. His estate later sued the hospital for malpractice, arguing he had been overloaded with intravenous fluids after being misdiagnosed as dehydrated; the case went to trial in 1991, and the hospital settled for $8 million without admitting liability.

A hand clutching an apple and a broken-off arm turned up in the same jumble of marble pieces, but museum staff in Paris judged that reattaching them, or guessing at any fuller repair, would do more harm than leaving the figure as it was found.

A base recovered near the statue bore a Greek signature crediting a sculptor named Alexandros, tied to a Carian river-valley city founded under the Seleucids. That piece was lost within a few years of the sculpture's arrival in Paris, and Alain Pasquier, who holds that curatorial post at the Louvre today, declines to certify that the signed fragment was really this statue's own base, rather than some other piece from the same jumbled find, so the credit stays probable rather than proven.

About 130 to 100 BC, per the dating the museum has settled on, reached by comparing the carving style against other Hellenistic sculpture rather than from any surviving document. The Athenian sculptor Praxiteles, credited with the era's first major unclothed rendering of the goddess of love, made a far grander namesake than pinning the work on a little-known carver working generations later, well past Greece's classical high point, and that is whose workshop museum leadership settled on for the newly unearthed figure. Auguste de Forbin was running the museum in those years, and he put that classical-era credit into print; the museum stood by it for generations even as the inscription argued for a later date.

before_faq: The Italian word behind it, rinascita, was first used in writing about art by Giorgio Vasari, in the preface to his 1550 biographical collection. It settled into the now-familiar English term much later, mainly through a Swiss historian's landmark 1860 study of Italian culture, five years after a French historian had already applied a similar word, in a much more science-heavy sense, back in 1855.

No. Vasari's biography of the two painters claimed Castagno murdered Veneziano to get his hands on a closely guarded oil-painting technique, then confessed the crime as his own life was ending, but Castagno died of plague on August 19, 1457, while Veneziano lived on for roughly another four years, until May 1461. The archivist Gaetano Milanesi, working a few centuries later, cross-checked financial documents against parish burial entries in an 1862 essay, showing the timeline simply could not have happened.

It is a collection of biographies covering Italy's architects, sculptors, and painters, first published in two volumes in 1550 and expanded to three volumes in a revised 1568 edition. It is generally treated as the founding text of Western art history, and the first book to frame the period's art in terms of rinascita, an Italian word for the rebirth of a lost classical standard.

Art historians generally place Renaissance art somewhere between the 1300s and the early 1600s, with its most influential period in Italy running from about 1400 to 1600. A landmark 1860 study, written by the Swiss scholar most often named as the one who put the modern label into general use, bracketed it more specifically, starting with the painter Giotto, active in the early 1300s, and ending with Michelangelo, who died in 1564.

For many of the artists Vasari wrote about, his book is the earliest or only surviving written account of their lives, so it remains a starting point by necessity. Modern historians treat individual claims in it, especially anecdotes about motive, character, and cause of death, as needing independent documentary corroboration rather than acceptance as fact, exactly the test the fabricated Veneziano killing failed to pass.

before_faq: Biographers stop short of calling it a proven medical or causal trigger, and both his drinking and his marital problems trace back well before the 1950 shoot. What is documented is a specific timeline: two dry years came to an end the night the filming wrapped, right around Thanksgiving 1950 (accounts vary on the precise day, some placing it on the holiday itself and others on the Saturday to either side), and did not stop again. Historians treat that night as the moment things shifted for good, not as a confirmed single cause of the car crash that killed him roughly six years after.

In narration recorded for Hans Namuth's 1951 film, Pollock walked through his method in plain, physical terms: he skipped any preparatory sketching, painted directly, and preferred laying the canvas flat on the floor so he could move around and feel closer to the work itself. He never used the term \"action painting\" himself; Harold Rosenberg, writing as a critic, coined it separately in a December 1952 essay.

His wife, Lee Krasner, said the numerical titles were meant to strip away suggestion: \"Numbers are neutral. They make people look at a painting for what it is, pure painting.\" Many of his numbered works carry a secondary, descriptive title added later by galleries or owners, which is why the same painting is sometimes cited two different ways.

The work, made using glass as the painting surface instead of canvas, carries the catalogue title No. 29, 1950, and is held today by a Canadian national museum in Ottawa. Pollock worked pebbles, beads, loose string, and bits of tinted glass into the wet paint, using both aluminum enamel and black enamel.

Pollock's death came late in the evening on August 11 of 1956, around a quarter past ten, when the Oldsmobile he was driving, drunk at the time, left the road barely a mile short of where he'd been living, the New York hamlet of Springs. He and one passenger, Edith Metzger, did not survive, while Ruth Kligman, riding with them, pulled through.

His record is $200 million, paid privately by hedge-fund manager Kenneth Griffin in 2015 for Number 17A (1948), bought along with a de Kooning from the David Geffen Foundation in a single $500 million deal. The previous benchmark, Number 5, 1948, had sold the same way for $140 million in 2006. Smaller drip paintings and works on paper sell for far less, from the low hundreds of thousands into the low millions depending on size and date.
